Chunk Practice

Break a fast passage into small chunks, link them up, and practise at changing tempos until it’s clean at speed.

Fast passages get learned in small pieces. Cut the passage into chunks, play each one at a tempo you can play clean, then link them together and bring the tempo up.

Press Play and play along. Every clean pass is a little faster; slip, and it slows a step. Changing tempos, rhythm variants, your own linking order.
The passage

Paste ABC, or take the piece from the Notation page.

Linking and tempos

bpm

Keys, pedals and what "clean" means

Space play / stop, M listen, Y clean, N not yet, ← → steps. "Clean" means right notes, right rhythm, no tension.

Pedals: Clean is the top key of an 88-key keyboard (C8) and Not yet the bottom key (A0). Change them, or bind a footswitch, with MIDI buttons in the top bar.

In Quick, saying nothing counts as clean, so one pedal (Not yet) is all you need.

With the click going round, answer any time during the pass or in the clicks after it. A missed stretch try costs nothing; a missed working try drops the tempo a step.

Best clean tempo for each step
Kept in this browser for this passage. Click a step to go to it.
For teachers: how it works
  1. Quick. Chunks link forwards; the click never stops; each clean pass is about a fifth of the way from 70% of the target to the target, a slip a step back. Saying nothing is a clean pass, so a student needs only to own up to the misses.
  2. Chunks. Small enough to play clean on the first or second try. Ending on the next chunk's first note practises the joins.
  3. Linking. Forwards: each new chunk alone, then with the one before, then everything so far. Backwards does the same from the end, so the end of the passage gets the most practice.
  4. Changing tempos (Full control). Each step cycles a working try, a slow try (two steps under), a working try, and a stretch (a step over). Clean working tries in a row raise the tempo a step; a clean stretch becomes the new working tempo. A linked step starts a little under the slowest of its chunks' best.
  5. Keyboard grading. With a MIDI keyboard each pass is checked note by note: the right key, within about a third of the shortest note's length (60–140 ms) of the click; a missed, wrong or extra note is not clean. A Clean / Not yet press overrides it.
  6. Rhythm variants. Long–short and short–long reshape pairs of equal notes, so each note gets a turn to be the long one.

Works Cited

For students

Kageyama, Noa. The Bulletproof Musician. bulletproofmusician.com/. A performance psychologist’s articles on practice research, written for players.

Lam, Ann. “Chunking and Piano.” Substack, annlam.substack.com/p/chunking-and-piano.

“Rhythm Practice Done Right.” Practising the Piano, practisingthepiano.com/rhythm-practice-done-right/.

For teachers

Allingham, Emma, and Clemens Wöllner. “Slow Practice and Tempo-Management Strategies in Instrumental Music Learning: Investigating Prevalence and Cognitive Functions.” Psychology of Music, 2022, doi:10.1177/03057356211073481. doi.org/10.1177/03057356211073481. Abstract and the university’s summary read.

Allingham, Emma. Slow Practice in Instrumental Music Learning. 2022. Universität Hamburg, PhD dissertation, ediss.sub.uni-hamburg.de/handle/ediss/9763. Summary read; title as listed there may differ slightly.

Barry, Nancy H. “The Effects of Practice Strategies, Individual Differences in Cognitive Style, and Gender upon Technical Accuracy and Musicality of Student Instrumental Performance.” Psychology of Music, vol. 20, no. 2, 1992, pp. 112–23. journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0305735692202002. Abstract read.

Carter, Christine E., and Jessica A. Grahn. “Optimizing Music Learning: Exploring How Blocked and Interleaved Practice Schedules Affect Advanced Performance.” Frontiers in Psychology, vol. 7, 2016, article 1251. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4989027.

Chaffin, Roger, and Gabriela Imreh. “‘Pulling Teeth and Torture’: Musical Memory and Problem Solving.” Thinking and Reasoning, vol. 3, no. 4, 1997, pp. 315–36. musiclab.uconn.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/290/2013/10/Pulling-Teeth-Chaffin-1997.pdf.

Duke, Robert A., Amy L. Simmons, and Carla Davis Cash. “It’s Not How Much; It’s How: Characteristics of Practice Behavior and Retention of Performance Skills.” Journal of Research in Music Education, vol. 56, no. 4, 2009, pp. 310–21. Read through a summary.

Stambaugh, Laura A. “When Repetition Isn’t the Best Practice Strategy: Effects of Blocked and Random Practice Schedules.” Journal of Research in Music Education, vol. 58, no. 4, 2011, pp. 368–83. Abstract read.

Wightman, Dennis C., and Gavan Lintern. “Part-Task Training of Tracking for Manual Control.” Human Factors, vol. 27, no. 3, 1985, pp. 267–83. Read through later reviews that cite it.
